steps.body:
You know the poll lands within about 2 SE of the truth, 95% of the time. Turn that around and the truth lies within about 2 SE of the poll.

That distance is the **margin of error**, and it turns a number into a band:

48% ± 3 → every value from 45% to 51% is plausible.

explanationVariants: 48 − 3 = 45 and 48 + 3 = 51, so the plausible values run from 45% to 51%.
The single number is only the middle of the band. The band is the finding.

widget.prompt: A poll reports 48% support with a margin of error of 3 points. Which statement is best supported?

options.label: Support is plausibly anywhere from 45% to 51%.
options.feedback: Right — the band is the result. The headline number is just its midpoint.

options.label: Support is exactly 48%.
options.feedback: That is the one thing the poll cannot say. It reported a band precisely because the estimate wobbles.

options.label: Support is definitely below 50%.
options.feedback: The band reaches 51%, so a true majority is squarely inside the plausible range.

options.label: Support is between 45% and 51% with certainty.
options.feedback: The method captures the truth about 95% of the time, not always. About 1 poll in 20 produces a band that misses entirely.

steps.body: The price of precision, drawn as a curve.

widget.prompt: A 400-person poll has a margin of about ±5 points. Roughly how many people would you need for a margin of about ±1 point?
widget.lowFeedback: Too few. Dividing the margin by 5 costs 5² = 25 times the sample, not 5 times.
widget.highFeedback: More people than you need. 400 × 25 = 10,000 already gets the margin down to about a point.
widget.successFeedback: About 10,000. Cutting the margin by a factor of 5 means multiplying the sample by 5² = 25 — precision is bought by the square, which is why ±1 polls are rare.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents si margin.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for si margin must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines si margin.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

predict.prompt: A 400-person poll carries a margin of about ±5 points. To reach about ±1 point you would need roughly…
predict.reveal: About twenty-five times — some 10,000 people. The margin shrinks with the SQUARE ROOT of the sample, so cutting it to a fifth costs 5² = 25 times the sample. That is why national polls stop near a thousand: the next point of precision is ruinously expensive.

explanationVariants: The margin is 2 × √(p(1−p)/n). Only n is under your control, and it sits under a square root.
A larger sample narrows the margin. A larger population does nothing, and a more careful interviewer does nothing to the ARITHMETIC — though it may reduce bias, which the margin never covered anyway.

widget.prompt: Which of these actually shrink the margin of error?

items.label: Polling 4× as many people
items.feedback: n rises fourfold, √n doubles, and the margin halves.

items.label: Polling in a smaller town
items.feedback: The population size never enters the formula. Only n does.

items.label: Asking the question more politely
items.feedback: That may reduce BIAS, which is worth doing — but the margin of error only ever measured random wobble, so it does not move.

items.label: Polling when the true split is far from 50/50
items.feedback: p(1−p) is largest at 0.5, so a lopsided truth gives a smaller SE. You cannot choose it, but it does shrink the margin.

widget.missFeedback: Look at what actually appears in 2 × √(p(1−p)/n): only p and n.
widget.successFeedback: n and p move the margin. Population size and politeness do not — one is absent from the formula, the other fights a different enemy.

steps.body:
The margin is honest about exactly one thing: **random sampling wobble**.

It assumes your sample was random and everyone answered truthfully. It cannot see undercoverage, nonresponse, or a leading question.

So ± 3 means *if the method is sound*, the truth is within 3 points. If the method leans, the ± is measuring the wrong thing.

explanationVariants: The margin is computed from n and p alone. Nothing in it knows who was left out of the frame.
A biased poll with a huge n reports a tiny margin — and that tiny margin is exactly what makes it dangerous.

widget.prompt: An online opt-in poll of 50,000 fans reports 91% ± 0.3%. What is wrong with quoting that margin?

options.label: Margin ignores self-selection bias
options.feedback: Right. It is arithmetic about the wrong problem — precise, and beside the point.

options.label: Margin is too small to be correct
options.feedback: The arithmetic is fine: with n = 50,000 the random wobble really is about ±0.3 points. That is the trap, not a mistake.

options.label: Margins require fewer than 10,000 responses
options.feedback: There is no such rule. The formula works at any n — it just never claimed to see bias.

options.label: Large samples make every poll trustworthy
options.feedback: Trust comes from the sampling method, not the head count. 50,000 self-selected fans are still 50,000 fans.

hints: Compute the standard error first: SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with p̂ = 0.48 and n = 1000.
0.48 × 0.52 = 0.2496; divide by 1000 and take the root to get about 0.0158.
Double it for the 95% margin, then convert to percentage points and round to one decimal.
explanationVariants: SE = √(0.2496/1000) ≈ 0.0158, so the margin is 2 × 0.0158 ≈ 0.0316 ≈ 3.2 percentage points.
This is where the familiar ±3 on a thousand-person poll comes from — the arithmetic barely changes for any p near a half.

widget.prompt: A poll of 1,000 people finds p̂ = 0.48. Find the 2-SE margin of error, in percentage points (one decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: That is one standard error. The 95% margin is two of them.
That is 4 × SE. The convention is a 2-SE band, which covers about 95% of the pile.
That is p̂(1 − p̂) as a percent. The division by n and the square root have not happened yet.

widget.fallbackFeedback: SE = √(0.48 × 0.52/1000) ≈ 0.0158; twice that is about 3.2 percentage points.

takeaways: Margin of error ≈ 2 × SE, and it turns a point estimate into a range of plausible values.
Only n (and, out of your control, p) move it — the population size does not.
The margin measures random wobble and nothing else. It is blind to bias by construction.
steps.teaser: Next: what the "95%" in "95% confident" is actually counting.

concept.body: Take the estimate, subtract the margin, add the margin — that is the band. Report the band, not the point. And remember what the band was built from: sampling wobble only, assuming the method itself was sound.

explanationVariants: 52 − 4 = 48, so the band runs from 48% to 56%.
The lower end is estimate minus margin: 52 − 4.

widget.prompt: A poll reports 52% with a margin of 4 points. What is the LOWER end of the plausible band, in percent?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the upper end (52 + 4). The lower end subtracts the margin.
That is the margin itself, not an end of the band. Apply it to the estimate: 52 − 4.
